metadata.title: Optimizing automated scoring in ILSAs with prompt compression

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses digital PIRLS 2021 multilingual responses from 27 countries, but it does not report applying PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights in the automated scoring evaluation. The analytic dataset is constructed by selecting a randomly sampled 20% subset of the full country-level digital PIRLS responses for computational feasibility, and then scoring responses with GPT-4o under different prompt-compression configurations. Because the task is automated scoring agreement (human vs machine) rather than estimating population parameters, the manuscript does not describe any complex-survey-weighted estimation. Analysts replicating this work should use the PIRLS-provided student/sampling weights if they intend to generalize agreement rates to the full national populations; otherwise, unweighted agreement evaluation is consistent with the paper’s focus on scoring accuracy and cost-efficiency.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use PIRLS achievement plausible values (PVs) or any PV-based cognitive outcome; instead, it evaluates automated scoring agreement for five 1-point constructed-response items using binary human vs machine scores. Missing-data handling is not described because the evaluation is based on the availability of multilingual responses and the ability to generate/parse JSON outputs; the paper does not report a missingness mechanism requiring imputation or deletion rules. Therefore, the missing-data strategy is a reporting gap for any cases with absent/failed model outputs or incomplete responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used digital PIRLS 2021 multilingual responses for five secured 1-point constructed-response (CR) “trend items” (four literary items from Passages A and C; one informational item from Passage B). The study restricts to medium-to-difficult passages and evaluates GPT-4o automated scoring under a generalized prompt template with (i) baseline prompts using original passages and original scoring guides (SGs), (ii) Model 1 using refined SGs, (iii) Model 2 using refined SGs plus passage summarization with extractive SG refinement (RefinedSG_ET), and (iv) Model 3 using refined SGs plus passage summarization with abstractive SG refinement (RefinedSG_AT). For feasibility, it further uses a randomly selected 20% subset of the full dataset for each country, while maintaining representation across countries and languages.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading — 1-point Constructed-Response (CR) items (5 items; multilingual, 27 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Automated scoring agreement (accuracy) vs human scoring
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (accuracy, %): Baseline avg 92.62% (κ=0.82); Model 1 avg 92.19% (κ=0.81); Model 2 avg 92.41% (κ=0.82); Model 3 avg 92.87% (κ=0.80). Item-level accuracy for Model 3: Item1 91.13%, Item2 90.26%, Item3 94.36%, Item4 94.85%, Item5 93.77%. Primary metric chosen as accuracy due to low-stakes binary 1-point items and skewed score distributions affecting κ.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading the study leveraged prompt compression and scoring-guide refinement (baseline vs refined SGs; passage summarization; extractive vs abstractive SG refinement) to predict automated scoring agreement with human scoring for five 1-point CR items, finding that Model 3 achieved the highest average accuracy (92.87%) while substantially compressing passages and SGs (to ~18% and ~15% of original lengths). This indicates that prompt compression can preserve (or slightly improve) automated scoring accuracy while reducing operational cost and complexity for multilingual PIRLS-style assessments, though the evaluation is based on a 20% subset and does not establish causal effects on learning outcomes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading — 1-point Constructed-Response (CR) items (5 items; multilingual, 27 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Inter-rater reliability (Cohen’s kappa) between automated and human scoring
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (κ): Baseline avg 0.82; Model 1 avg 0.81; Model 2 avg 0.82; Model 3 avg 0.80. Item-level κ for Model 3: Item1 0.82, Item2 0.81, Item3 0.81, Item4 0.85, Item5 0.73.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading the study leveraged prompt compression and scoring-guide refinement to predict automated scoring agreement reliability (Cohen’s kappa) with human scoring for five 1-point CR items, finding that Model 3’s κ (avg 0.80) was slightly lower than the baseline and Model 2 (avg 0.82) despite comparable accuracy. This indicates that while compressed prompts can maintain practical agreement, κ may be sensitive to skewed item difficulty and chance agreement, so operational adoption should consider both accuracy and reliability diagnostics rather than relying on a single metric.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading — 1-point Constructed-Response (CR) items (5 items; multilingual, 27 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Hallucination rate in automated scoring outputs
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model comparison (hallucination rate, %): Baseline avg 0.05%; Model 1 avg 0.69%; Model 2 avg 0.47%; Model 3 avg 0.12%. Item-level hallucination for Model 3: Item1 0.08%, Item2 0.08%, Item3 0.14%, Item4 0.24%, Item5 0.08%. Hallucinations were detected via translation-length ratio thresholds (2.2 for Latin-alphabet languages; 20 for non-Latin scripts) and then corrected by setting machine score to 0.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading the study leveraged prompt compression and refined scoring-guide strategies to predict hallucination rates in GPT-4o automated scoring for five 1-point CR items, finding that Model 3 reduced hallucinations substantially relative to Model 1 and Model 2 (avg 0.12% vs 0.69% and 0.47%) while remaining close to the baseline (0.05%). This indicates that carefully designed question-specific summarization plus abstractive SG refinement can improve cost-efficiency without materially increasing hallucination risk, though hallucination detection is heuristic and may miss some error modes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading — 1-point Constructed-Response (CR) items (5 items; multilingual, 27 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Cost-efficiency of automated scoring (running time and cost per item)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Running time & cost (Model 3 vs baseline): Model 3 average cost ≈ $3.62 per item vs baseline $15–17 per item (reported as ~76% cost reduction). Running time for Model 3 average ≈ 0:38:55 per item (item times: 0:31:54 to 0:49:33). Compression of passages and SGs is performed once per item at ~ $0.50 and requires 1–2 seconds.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Digital (Grade 4) Reading the study leveraged prompt compression (question-specific passage summaries and refined SGs) to predict cost-efficiency of automated scoring, finding that Model 3 achieved an average cost of about $3.62 per item compared with $15–17 for the baseline while keeping running time only slightly shorter. This indicates that prompt compression can make LLM-based automated scoring operationally feasible for large-scale multilingual ILSAs by reducing token-driven API expenses, though the cost estimates depend on the specific API pricing and the study’s 20% evaluation subset.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates GPT-4o-based automated scoring for five secured 1-point constructed-response items from digital PIRLS 2021 (Grade 4) across 27 countries and 29 languages, using a randomly selected 20% subset per country for feasibility. It compares a baseline prompt (original passages and original scoring guides) against three prompt-compression configurations: refined scoring guides (Model 1), passage summarization plus extractive SG refinement (Model 2), and passage summarization plus abstractive SG refinement (Model 3). Model 3 achieved the highest average accuracy (92.87%) with κ=0.80, closely approximating the baseline (92.62%, κ=0.82), while keeping hallucination rates low (0.12% vs 0.05% baseline). The paper also reports a major efficiency gain: average cost about $3.62 per item versus $15–17 for the baseline (~76% reduction). Limitations include heuristic hallucination detection, lack of reported missing-data handling, and no explicit use of PIRLS sampling/replicate weights for generalizing agreement rates.
